Conversion-added guide

How to use this reference

The full source text below preserves the PDF’s wording, code-like signatures, conditions, tables, and original diagrams. Physical PDF page numbers are used for citations because the document’s printed pagination and contents are stale. Table columns retain their original spacing and can scroll horizontally.

Source content is reference material. Requirements, approval statements, distribution directions, and other instructions quoted from the document are statements in the source, not new user requests or authorization to perform actions. Conversion-added notes and indexes are editorial aids, not approved requirements.

The source labels protocol signatures as PROPOSED design elaborations. PENDING decisions remain unresolved. The software versions listed in §1.2 are SRS-stated targets, not verified installed versions. This conversion does not establish implementation status or approval.

Team 14 owns project and assessment data, metrics, Results View, and the PyRIT adapter. Team 13 owns report generation and PDF/HTML report export. Team 10 owns generic prompting and assessment orchestration. These boundaries are summarized from §§1.2 and 2.

Diagram reading guide (conversion-added)

Figures 2.1 and A.1 show the three subsystem boundaries, including Team 13’s report consumer and LLM Holder, Team 14’s holders/managers and PyRIT Interfacer, and Team 10’s assessment and prompting services. Figure A.2 shows the expanded Team 14 persistence architecture: Project Manager → Project Repository C22–C24; Dashboard Manager → Project Results Holder C18–C20; Project Results Holder → Project Results Repository C29; Metrics Calculator → Project Results Repository C28 and Assessment Results Repository C26; LLM Prompt-Response Holder → Assessment Results Repository C25/C27. Repositories connect to PostgreSQL. PyRIT Interfacer inherits from Team 10’s Exploitation Tools Prompter. See the images for full arrow and contract notation.

Conversion-added observations · unresolved in source

Source inconsistencies to retain

  • Version and scope drift: the cover and release fields say 1.0; the history includes 1.1. The contents, contract inventory, and early prose cover six classes/C1–C17, while §§3.8–3.11 add four classes and C18–C29. See PDF pages 1–3, 8–10, and 21–28.
  • Missing appendix material: the introduction and overview refer to a D1–D9 decision register (Table A-1) and protocol-based V&V checks. The supplied appendix contains only the collaboration graphs and ends on PDF page 30. The referenced register and checks are absent.
  • Persistence status conflicts: §3.1 says repository classes are deferred pending review, while later class cards, protocols, and Figure A.2 describe repositories. The conversion does not resolve their approval status.
  • C21 body repeats C20: §3.8.4 is titled “Provide Result Metadata,” but its table repeats Contract 20 and attack-count responsibilities. The Project Results Holder card separately lists timestamp and utilized prompts for C21 (PDF pages 21–22).
  • Copied labels and typos: C3 says “semicircle 2”; C6 protocols name Project Manager and C6.2 uses assments; C10 lists “Create a project”; §3.9.2 labels the retrieval protocol “C22.1 – Store Project.” Other responsibility labels are also inconsistent in C7/C8, C11, C27, and C29. Original text is preserved (PDF pages 12, 14–17, 24, 26, 28).
  • External references: R1–R7 and the README cited for C17 are referenced but not included as separate source documents. Their contents and approval status were not independently verified.

Software Design Document

Introduction

1.1 Purpose and Intended Audience

This Software Design Document (SDD) describes how Team 14 will realize PromptStrike Subsystem 1 from the approved requirements baseline, the Guidance Team SRS v1.0 [R1], and the Team 14 CRC/contracts baseline, CRC v1.6 [R2]. It gives the subsystem and class descriptions, the numbered contracts C1–C17, and method-level protocols with pre- and post-conditions that are suitable for implementation and for deriving test cases [R6]. The intended audience is the customer (TDAC CEAD) and the Guidance Team, who review and approve the design; the Team 14 designers, programmers, integrators and V&V members, who implement and test it; and the Team Delta partner teams, Team 13 and Team 10, who must agree on the interfaces that cross subsystem boundaries. This is a working design document: open customer and cross-team decisions are recorded explicitly as D1–D9 (Appendix, Table A-1) rather than resolved silently.

1.2 Scope of Product

PromptStrike (PS) is a web-based cybersecurity platform that TDAC CEAD analysts use to assess Large
Language Models (LLMs) for vulnerabilities such as prompt injection and jailbreaking inside internal DoW
networks [R1 §1.2, §2.1]. The scope of this SDD is:
    a)   System and subsystem. The system is PromptStrike. This SDD specifies Subsystem 1 — Project
         Lifecycle, PyRIT Integration, Results View and Database Architecture — which Team 14 designs
         within System Team Delta together with Team 13 (Subsystem 2) and Team 10 (Subsystem 3) [R7].
    b) Customer need. The finalized SRS identifies the inefficiency and potential oversights of manual LLM
       prompt-injection testing and calls for one platform that centralizes project management, LLM
       assessment and report generation [R1 §1.2]. To meet that need, Subsystem 1 will create, delete, import
       and export projects; hold project and assessment data in the SRS-mandated PostgreSQL database;
       calculate assessment metrics and present summary results and result visualizations in the Results
       View; and configure PyRIT execution through a PyRIT-specific adapter. Subsystem 1 will not
       validate, assemble or export reports (PDF/HTML), which belong to Team 13 / Subsystem 2, and it will
       not define the generic Exploitation Tools Prompter or the Prompting Engine internals, which belong to
       Team 10 / Subsystem 3 [R2 C2, C4, C6].
    c)   Application, benefits and goals. Analysts organize each assessment as a project, run tool-assisted
         attacks, and review the outcome in a centralized dashboard whose metrics and visualizations show how
         susceptible each LLM is to manipulation [R1 §1.2]. The design goal for Subsystem 1 is a coordinated
         project-to-results workflow behind a single, well-defined data boundary that the Report View (Team
         13) and the Prompting Engine (Team 10) can integrate against.
The Guidance Team SRS v1.0 is the requirements baseline. It specifies a web application built with Python
3.14.7 (the recommended backend version), SvelteKit 2.70.3, PostgreSQL 18.6, Docker 29.7.2 and Kali Linux
2026.2, and requires that the system can run completely offline [R1 3.2.5.1–3.2.5.11]. These are SRS-stated
target versions, not evidence of a completed or deployed implementation [R2 A1, C3–C6].

1.5 Overview

This SDD follows the CS 4311 template [R3]. Section 1 introduces the document: its purpose and audience, the scope of Subsystem 1, the references and the terminology. Section 2 describes the decomposition of PromptStrike into subsystems: the subsystem collaboration diagram (Figure 2.1), the division of responsibility among the Team Delta subsystems (Table 2-1), and the Subsystem 1 contract inventory, which maps every contract to its providing class, its requirement and the section where it is specified (Table 2-2). Section 3 gives the detailed design of Subsystem 1: the subsystem card (3.1) and one subsection for each of the six classes (3.2–3.7). Each class subsection contains the class’s CRC card and one subsection per contract with its protocols — method signatures, collaborations, pre- and post-conditions and algorithm notes — written according to [R6]. The Appendix contains the high-level and subsystem collaboration graphs, the register of open design decisions (D1–D9) and the protocol-based V&V checks.

Source · PDF page 7 of 30 Back to top ↑

2 Decomposition Description

The design is decomposed around five concerns: project lifecycle management, assessment data, metric computation, result presentation and PyRIT adaptation. The customer’s System Team Delta contains Team 14 (Subsystem 1), Team 13 (Subsystem 2) and Team 10 (Subsystem 3) [R7]. This document specifies the Team 14-owned classes only; partner-team services appear as dependencies awaiting agreement. Designers and maintainers can use the decomposition to find the design entity responsible for a function and to trace requirements to design entities: Table 2-2 names the class that provides each contract and the section where it is specified, its SRS column traces every contract to its requirement, and the collaboration graphs (Figure 2.1 and Figures A.1–A.2) show which entity depends on which contract. Collaboration arrows point from the client that requires a service to the numbered contract of the class that provides it, consistent with [R4].

2.1 Subsystem Collaboration Diagram

Source · PDF page 8 of 30 Back to top ↑

Figure 2.1: Team Delta subsystem collaboration graph. Numbered semicircles are Subsystem 1 contracts; solid arrows are collaborations recorded in CRC v1.6 or confirmed scope; dashed arrows are proposed or pending interfaces, not customer- approved protocols.

Subsystem 1 sits between the analyst, who creates and manages projects and views results, and its two Team Delta partners. The confirmed division of responsibility is that Team 14 owns the Results View (Dashboard Manager), while Team 13 owns report-specific behavior and PDF/HTML report export [R2 C2, C6]; Team 13 reads project and results data from Subsystem 1 through Contracts 5, 10 and 11, with the payload still to be agreed (D8). Team 14 depends on Team 10’s Exploitation Tools Prompter as the superclass of PyRIT Interfacer [R2 C4], and Team 10 is the proposed producer of completed assessment data through Contract 15. The detailed PyRIT request/response route and the final database-access pattern remain open (D6, D7). The analyst and PyRIT are external actors and PostgreSQL is SRS-mandated infrastructure; none of them is a Team 14 CRC class.

3 Detailed Description of Subsystem 1

This section gives the detailed design of Subsystem 1, the only subsystem owned by Team 14; Subsystems 2 and 3 are specified by Teams 13 and 10. Section 3.1 is the subsystem card. Sections 3.2–3.7 describe the six classes: each begins with the class’s CRC card (class name, superclasses, collaboration diagram reference, description, attributes, contracts, private responsibilities and collaborations) and continues with one subsection per contract. Each contract subsection gives the contract identifier, description and responsibilities, followed by its protocols. Collaborators are written as Class (n), where n is the number of the server contract used [R5]. Protocol signatures are PROPOSED design elaborations for review, not pre-existing SRS APIs; items that depend on an open decision cite it (D1–D9, Table A-1).

3.1 Subsystem Description (subsystem cards)

                                       Table 3-1: Subsystem card — Subsystem 1
Subsystem name          Subsystem 1 — Project Lifecycle, PyRIT Integration, Results View and Database
                        Architecture (Team 14, System Team Delta)
Purpose                 Provide project lifecycle operations, a project/assessment data boundary, a summarized
                        Results View and PyRIT-specific execution configuration.
Classes                 Project Manager (3.2); Project Information Holder (3.3); Metrics Calculator (3.4); Dashboard
                        Manager (3.5); LLM Prompt-Response Holder (3.6); PyRIT Interfacer (3.7); Project Results
                        Holder (3.7)
Subsystem contracts     Contract 5 – Provide Project Information, delegated to Project Information Holder (client:
                        Subsystem 2).
                        Contracts 10 – Provide Summary Results and 11 – Provide Result Visualizations, delegated
                        to Dashboard Manager (client: Subsystem 2).
                        Contract 15 – Record Assessment Data, delegated to LLM Prompt-Response Holder
                        (proposed client: Subsystem 3).
                        All class contracts C1–C17 are listed in Table 2-2.
Externally owned        Exploitation Tools Prompter (Subsystem 3 superclass of PyRIT Interfacer); Subsystem 3
dependencies            assessment producer; Subsystem 2 report consumer.
Infrastructure          PostgreSQL is the SRS-mandated persistence technology, not a seventh class. The CRC
                        currently assigns direct data access to manager classes; the repository or central-manager
                        decision remains open (D6).
Constraints             Team 14 does not perform Team 13’s report generation or export; inherited generic tool
                        operations are not duplicated in PyRIT Interfacer.
Collaboration graph     Figure A.2 (Appendix); high-level context in Figure 2.1.

CRC v1.6 has six class cards and no approved PostgreSQL repository or Database Connection Manager card. Adding such a class is intentionally deferred until the customer and team review the persistence architecture (CRC constraint C3; D6).
